tasks.description: Proofread articles — The Church Fathers on the Eucharist

result.name: The Church Fathers on the Eucharist

debates.before: wrote seven letters to churches across Asia Minor
debates.after: wrote seven surviving letters, mostly to churches in Asia Minor, as well as one to the church at Rome and one to Polycarp
debates.concern: The seven authentic letters traditionally attributed to Ignatius were not all addressed to churches in Asia Minor: one was addressed to the church at Rome and one to Polycarp personally.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Revise the description to reflect the destinations of the seven surviving letters.
debates.comment: The revision is more precise and corrects the misattribution of all seven letters to churches in Asia Minor.

debates.before: instructed new converts preparing for baptism in a series of lectures delivered during Holy Week
debates.after: instructed newly baptized Christians in a series of mystagogical lectures delivered during Easter week
debates.concern: Cyril's Mystagogical Catecheses were addressed to the newly baptized after their initiation, not to converts preparing for baptism during Holy Week.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Identify the audience as newly baptized Christians and place the lectures after baptism during Easter week.
debates.comment: An important liturgical and historical distinction; Cyril's Mystagogical Catecheses were indeed given to the newly baptized during Easter week.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Birth of Christ

debates.section: A Date Anchored in History, If Not Precisely
debates.before: The Church has nonetheless always reckoned its calendar from Dionysius's date, and by the fourth century had fixed December 25 in the West as the liturgical commemoration of the Nativity.
debates.after: The Western Christian calendar eventually adopted Dionysius's dating system, although other Christian traditions have used different calendar eras; by the fourth century, Rome had established December 25 as the liturgical commemoration of the Nativity.
debates.concern: The word "always" is inaccurate: Dionysius's era was adopted gradually and has not been the calendar era used by every Christian tradition. The original wording also compresses the history of the December 25 observance into a claim about the Church as a whole.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the adoption of Dionysius's dating system and specify Rome or the Western Church when describing the fourth-century December 25 observance.
debates.comment: The revision correctly avoids the historical inaccuracy of 'always' regarding Dionysius's system and clarifies the Western origin of December 25.

debates.before: a mission that begins in earnest at Pentecost, thirty-three years later.
debates.after: a mission that begins in earnest at Pentecost, roughly three decades later.
debates.concern: The exact interval between Jesus' birth and Pentecost is uncertain because both the date of the Nativity and the chronology of Jesus' public ministry and death are debated. Presenting Pentecost as exactly thirty-three years later is unnecessarily precise.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the exact interval with an approximate expression, or qualify it as a traditional chronology.
debates.comment: Switching to 'roughly three decades later' avoids false precision on an unresolved chronological point.

Proofread articles — Resurrection & Ascension

debates.before: He appeared to the assembled Eleven in the upper room, twice, a week apart, so that the doubting Thomas could touch His wounds.
debates.after: He appeared to the assembled disciples in the upper room, first without Thomas and then, a week later, with Thomas present so that he could touch Christ's wounds.
debates.concern: According to John 20:19–29, Thomas was absent from the first appearance in the upper room, so the first gathering was not the assembled Eleven. The sentence also incorrectly makes it sound as though the first appearance occurred specifically so Thomas could touch Christ's wounds.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Identify the first gathering as the disciples assembled without Thomas and the second as the gathering at which Thomas was present.
debates.comment: The revision correctly notes Thomas's absence from the first appearance, preventing a contradiction of John 20.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Our Lady of the Pillar

debates.before: Traditional — papal approbation; feast of Our Lady of the Pillar, 12 October
debates.after: Traditional — liturgical recognition; feast of Our Lady of the Pillar, 12 October
debates.concern: The article explicitly says that this apostolic-era apparition is not formally approved in the modern canonical sense. Calling its status “papal approbation” is therefore misleading and may suggest a formal approval that the article denies. The fact should describe the tradition's liturgical recognition without implying a modern canonical approval.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace “papal approbation” with wording describing the shrine's liturgical recognition or established devotion, unless a specific papal act of approbation is documented.
debates.comment: Accurate correction to avoid contradicting the article's own stance on canonical approval.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Council of Jerusalem

debates.before: Paul would later defend this decision at length in his Letter to the Galatians.
debates.after: Paul would later defend the freedom of Gentile believers from circumcision in his Letter to the Galatians.
debates.concern: Galatians strongly defends Gentile freedom from circumcision and the Mosaic Law, but it does not explicitly mention the Jerusalem decree. The original wording presents a disputed relationship between Galatians and Acts 15 as certain and may imply that Paul was directly defending the council's specific four requirements.
debates.suggestedCorrection: State the related Pauline teaching without claiming that Galatians directly defends the specific decision or decree described in Acts 15.
debates.comment: The revision avoids the theological oversimplification linking Galatians directly to the specific Jerusalem decree.

debates.before: Why, then, are you now putting God to the test by placing on the shoulders of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?
debates.after: Why, then, are you now putting God to the test by placing on the shoulders of the disciples a yoke that neither our ancestors nor we have been able to bear?
debates.concern: The quotation is attributed to the NABRE, but the NABRE wording uses "our ancestors," not "our fathers." As presented, this is not an exact quotation from the named translation.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace "our fathers" with "our ancestors," or identify the translation that actually uses the supplied wording.
debates.comment: Corrects an inaccurate quotation attribution by aligning the text precisely with the NABRE translation.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Persecution under Nero

debates.before: It was the see that Peter and Paul had both led and died for
debates.after: It was the city in which Peter and Paul both ministered and were martyred
debates.concern: The wording implies that Peter and Paul both led the Roman see. Peter is traditionally regarded as the first bishop of Rome, but Paul was an apostle and missionary who ministered in Rome, not a co-holder or successive leader of its episcopal see.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Distinguish Paul's ministry in Rome from Peter's traditional episcopal leadership of the Roman church.
debates.comment: A meaningful theological and historical correction, as Paul did not lead the see of Rome.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Destruction of the Temple

debates.before: marked the effective end of Second Temple Judaism
debates.after: marked the end of the Second Temple period and transformed Jewish religious life
debates.concern: The destruction ended the Temple-centered sacrificial system and is conventionally used to mark the end of the Second Temple period, but calling it the effective end of Second Temple Judaism can misleadingly suggest that Jewish religious identity or communal life ended immediately. Jewish life and interpretation continued and developed in multiple forms after AD 70.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use periodization language and describe the destruction's major transformation of Judaism without implying an instantaneous end to Jewish religious life.
debates.comment: An important nuance preventing the misconception that Judaism itself ceased to exist after the Temple fell.

debates.before: See ye all these things? Amen I say to you, there shall not be left here a stone upon a stone.
debates.after: You see all these things? Amen I say to you, there shall not be left here a stone upon a stone.
debates.concern: The quotation appears not to match the Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 24:2, which begins "You see all these things?" The current wording may be a conflation with another translation or Gospel wording while being specifically attributed to Douay-Rheims.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Check the quotation against the cited Douay-Rheims edition and replace it with the exact text, or identify the translation actually used.
debates.comment: Corrects the Douay-Rheims translation text accurately.

debates.before: End of Second Temple Judaism; fulfillment of Christ's prophecy of the Temple's fall
debates.after: End of the Second Temple period; interpreted by Christians as fulfillment of Christ's prophecy of the Temple's fall
debates.concern: The first clause is too compressed and can imply that Judaism itself ended in AD 70. The second presents a Christian theological interpretation as an unqualified historical significance. The article should distinguish conventional historical periodization from Christian interpretation.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Use wording that identifies the end of the Second Temple period and explicitly marks the prophecy's fulfillment as a Christian interpretation.
debates.comment: Correctly attributes the theological interpretation as such rather than stating it as a neutral historical fact.

tasks.description: Proofread articles — Persecution under Domitian

debates.section: Suspicion at the Heart of the Court
debates.before: The Roman historian Tertullian remembered Domitian as a man who inherited a portion of Nero's own cruelty
debates.after: The Christian writer Tertullian portrayed Domitian as a ruler who inherited a portion of Nero's own cruelty
debates.concern: Tertullian was a Christian apologist and theologian, not a Roman historian. The description is materially misleading about the nature of the source.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Identify Tertullian accurately as a Christian writer or apologist, and avoid presenting his account as that of a Roman historian.
debates.comment: Tertullian is indeed a Christian apologist rather than a traditional Roman historian, making the revision more accurate.

debates.section: Suspicion at the Heart of the Court
debates.before: by the final years of his reign (AD 81–96) that cruelty had turned decisively against the Christians of the empire. Unlike Nero's persecution, confined largely to the city of Rome in the aftermath of the Great Fire, Domitian's suspicion reached into the very heart of the imperial court itself.
debates.after: In the later years of his reign, Domitian became associated in Christian tradition with hostility toward some Christians and toward members of the imperial household. Unlike Nero's persecution, which is explicitly associated with Rome after the Great Fire, the extent and character of any broader persecution under Domitian remain debated.
debates.concern: The passage presents a large-scale, empire-wide persecution and a decisive policy shift as established fact. The surviving evidence is limited and does not clearly establish an organized empire-wide persecution under Domitian.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the scope and certainty of Domitian's actions, distinguishing the documented executions of particular elites from the later Christian tradition of a general persecution.
debates.comment: The revision correctly avoids presenting empire-wide persecution under Domitian as an established historical fact.

debates.before: Among the most notable victims of what the early Church remembered as its Second Persecution were figures of genuine political standing.
debates.after: Among the figures later associated with Christian persecution under Domitian were men of genuine political standing.
debates.concern: “Second Persecution” is a later traditional classification rather than an uncontested historical description of a clearly organized second empire-wide persecution. The passage also risks implying that the religious identity and persecution of both men are equally well established.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Describe this as a later Christian memory or tradition and distinguish the evidence for the individual cases.
debates.comment: Framing the 'Second Persecution' as part of later tradition rather than an uncontested fact is historically rigorous.

debates.before: Both were condemned, according to the ancient historian Dio Cassius, on charges of "atheism," the standard Roman accusation against those who abandoned the state religion for what officials regarded as a strange and dangerous foreign superstition.
debates.after: Dio Cassius reports that both were condemned on a charge translated as “atheism,” but the surviving evidence does not establish with equal certainty that both cases involved Christianity or that this was a standard accusation used in the precise way described here.
debates.concern: Dio Cassius uses the charge of atheism in connection with Domitian's condemnation of Flavius Clemens and Glabrio, but the identification of both men as Christians and the characterization of atheism as a standard formula for Christians are debated. The sentence overstates what the source establishes.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Separate Dio's report of the charge from the later or disputed identification of the defendants as Christians, and qualify the explanation of Roman religious accusations.
debates.comment: The revision correctly notes the scholarly debate surrounding the precise application of the charge of atheism to Christians.

debates.before: Ancient and consistent tradition places him in exile on the small Aegean island of Patmos during Domitian's reign's final year.
debates.after: Ancient Christian tradition places him in exile on the small Aegean island of Patmos during Domitian's reign, although the precise date is uncertain.
debates.concern: The Patmos exile is an ancient Christian tradition, but identifying it specifically with the final year of Domitian's reign is not established by the cited biblical text and should not be stated as certain.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Retain the traditional association with Domitian while removing the unsupported precision about the final year.
debates.comment: Dating the Patmos exile precisely to the final year of Domitian's reign is indeed a matter of tradition rather than certainty.

debates.before: It was on this same barren island, tradition holds, that John received the extraordinary visions that would become the Book of Revelation. They formed a message of hope and ultimate victory, composed remarkably in the very moment and place of the empire's attempt to silence its author.
debates.after: It was on this same island, tradition holds, that John received the extraordinary visions recorded in the Book of Revelation. The book presents a message of hope and ultimate victory; its precise date and circumstances of composition remain subjects of historical discussion.
debates.concern: The first sentence appropriately signals tradition, but the next sentence treats the date, circumstances, and imperial motive as established facts. Revelation 1:9 identifies Patmos and the reason given by the speaker, but does not by itself establish that the Roman government was attempting to silence the author at that precise moment.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Keep the theological interpretation, but qualify the historical reconstruction of the date, composition, and imperial motive.
debates.comment: The revision properly contextualizes the circumstances and date of Revelation's composition as matters of ongoing discussion.

debates.before: Domitian's persecution ended as abruptly as it had begun: assassinated in a palace conspiracy on 18 September, AD 96, he was succeeded by the elderly senator Nerva.
debates.after: The hostility toward Christians traditionally associated with Domitian ended with his assassination in a palace conspiracy on 18 September AD 96; he was succeeded by the elderly senator Nerva.
debates.concern: Domitian's assassination and Nerva's succession are established, but the sentence assumes that a clearly defined imperial persecution began and ended with those events. The evidence for such an organized persecution is disputed.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Preserve the secure political chronology while qualifying the historical reality and scope of Domitian's alleged persecution.
debates.comment: Replacing the notion of a formal persecution starting and stopping with political events improves historical accuracy.

debates.before: Nerva discontinued the persecution and recalled the exiles — among them, by the Church's ancient memory, John himself, who returned at last to resume his ministry at Ephesus.
debates.after: Christian tradition later associated Nerva's reign with the end of Domitianic hostility and the return of some exiles; it also traditionally holds that John eventually returned to Ephesus.
debates.concern: The claim that Nerva formally discontinued a persecution and recalled John is not securely documented. John's return to Ephesus is an ancient tradition, but the sentence combines several traditional elements as though they were established administrative actions and a documented event.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Mark Nerva's role and John's return as tradition, and avoid asserting that Nerva officially recalled John unless a specific reliable source supports it.
debates.comment: The claim that Nerva formally recalled exiles is poorly documented; the revised version is more appropriately cautious.

debates.before: c. AD 95-96 (final year of Domitian's reign)
debates.after: Later years of Domitian's reign; precise span uncertain
debates.concern: The stated final-year date presents a disputed chronology as precise fact. The article itself does not establish that the associated persecution or John's exile began in AD 95 and ended in AD 96.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Replace the precise span with a qualified date range, or verify it against the specific historical tradition being used.
debates.comment: A Quick Facts box should reflect scholarly uncertainty rather than presenting a contested date as exact.

debates.before: Accusations of 'atheism' — refusal of state religion and emperor worship
debates.after: Charge of “atheism” reported in connection with some cases; its relationship to Christianity and emperor worship is debated
debates.concern: The fact line converts a reported charge into a standardized explanation and implies that the cases uniformly concerned refusal of emperor worship. The ancient evidence and the defendants' Christian identity are not equally certain.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Qualify the charge and distinguish the surviving report from later interpretations of what it meant in these cases.
debates.comment: The revision avoids oversimplifying the charge of atheism as a standardized formula for emperor worship in these specific cases.

debates.before: Flavius Clemens; Manius Acilius Glabrio; exile of St. John to Patmos
debates.after: Flavius Clemens; Manius Acilius Glabrio; traditional association of St. John with exile on Patmos
debates.concern: The wording places John's Patmos exile alongside the named political figures as an equivalent established victim of the persecution. John's exile under Domitian is an ancient tradition, but its precise historical circumstances and connection to an organized persecution remain debated.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Label John's exile as traditional and distinguish it from the separately attested political cases.
debates.comment: Distinguishing between historical political figures and traditional associations for St. John is a necessary correction.

debates.before: Domitian's assassination, AD 96; Nerva recalled the exiles
debates.after: Domitian's assassination, AD 96; later Christian tradition associates Nerva's reign with the return of exiles
debates.concern: Domitian's assassination is secure, but the claim that Nerva recalled the exiles is presented too categorically. The surviving evidence does not clearly document a general recall of Christian exiles by Nerva.
debates.suggestedCorrection: Retain the secure assassination date and qualify the claim about Nerva and the exiles as tradition.
debates.comment: Attributing Nerva's recall of exiles to later tradition rather than established fact corrects an unproven administrative claim.
